{"id": "2:45/q01", "question": "Who is addressed by the command?", "turns_on": "Whether the surrounding Israelite discourse continues, shifts, or states a general command.", "positions": [{"id": "2:45/q01/p1", "position": "The Israelites or People of the Book are addressed; the instruction can also apply to others.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi and Razi prefer continuity with the surrounding Israelite address; Ibn Ashur cites the conjunction and 2:43. Tabarsi and Ibn Kathir extend its instruction generally. Razi says Jews knew the shared essence of patience and prayer despite differing ritual forms. Ibn Ashur says the passage also indirectly praises Muslims."}, {"id": "2:45/q01/p2", "position": "The address turns to Muslims or believers in Muhammad.", "reasons": "Al-Jubba'i and Abu Ali propose a change of audience; Razi's reported argument is that rejecters of the religion's prayer would not be addressed with it. Al-Wahidi, Razi, and Ibn Ashur favor the contextual Israelite reading over this shift."}, {"id": "2:45/q01/p3", "position": "All morally responsible people are addressed.", "reasons": "Tabarsi prefers this because nothing restricts the wording, while conceding that the preceding and following context concerns the People of the Book."}]}
{"id": "2:45/q02", "question": "For what are patience and prayer sought as help?", "turns_on": "The command leaves its object unstated; sources supply the preceding duties, ultimate reward, present needs, or a particular obstacle.", "positions": [{"id": "2:45/q02/p1", "position": "For obeying God's commands and abandoning sin, including the preceding covenant duties and accepting Muhammad.", "reasons": "Tabari ties this to the Book's covenant, losing leadership, and worldly attachment; Zajjaj, Wahidi, Razi, Biqai, Ibn Ashur, and Kur'an Yolu explain resistance to status, bribes, habits, and inherited error. Jishumi lists prayer, alms, prohibitions, covenant and the messengers' promise as possible omitted objects. Ghazali's account in Ibn Ashur sets religious motive against appetite."}, {"id": "2:45/q02/p2", "position": "For attaining the Hereafter, God's pleasure, mercy, or reward.", "reasons": "Muqatil details the five prayer times; the Durr version adds recitation, postures, takbir, tashahhud and blessings. Abu al-Aliya calls both acts obedience, Ibn Jurayj two aids to mercy. The Muslim-address interpretation seeks Paradise."}, {"id": "2:45/q02/p3", "position": "For distress, calamity, needs, and the good of this life and the next.", "reasons": "Baghawi, Kashshaf, Baydawi and others apply the command to affliction; Tabatabai says human strength fails before some tasks and God supplies the true aid. Elmalili emphasizes trust that changing hardship will pass. Some explain patience as awaiting relief."}, {"id": "2:45/q02/p4", "position": "For establishing religion, certainty, devotion, and spiritual realities.", "reasons": "Sahl names steadfast certainty; Ibn Ata the depths of reality; Abu Uthman time free for devotion. Qushayri and Qashani construe aid as maintaining divine presence and service amid overwhelming unveilings."}, {"id": "2:45/q02/p5", "position": "Specifically to avoid taking bribes for altering religion.", "reasons": "Jishumi reports a reading that addresses Jews taking money from followers and directs them to seek relief instead."}]}
{"id": "2:45/q03", "question": "How does the wording of 'seek help through patience' work?", "turns_on": "The syntactic scope of the imperative and the unspoken object.", "positions": [{"id": "2:45/q03/p1", "position": "It is an imperative; the prepositional phrase expresses an instrument or cause, and the object of help is omitted for generality.", "reasons": "Al-Samin derives استعينوا from استعونوا with a seeking sīn and notes direct or bā-mediated government, with bā also able to mean accompaniment; Nahhas parses الصبر as genitive. Akhfash discusses coordinated predicates, distinguishing wāw from aw with 9:62, 62:11, 28:73, 4:112 and several poems."}, {"id": "2:45/q03/p2", "position": "The command joins the earlier imperatives despite intervening clauses.", "reasons": "Al-Samin treats it as coordinated with the preceding commands."}]}

{"id": "2:45/q06", "question": "What special value or scope is assigned to patience?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:45/q06/p1", "position": "Patience underlies faith and moral success and receives exceptional reward.", "reasons": "Qurtubi and Bursevi contrast tenfold deeds, multiplied charity, and reward without measure for patience (6:160, 2:261, 39:10, 42:43); some tie this to fasting and the divine report that God rewards it. Ali likens patience to faith's head; Umar and Maymun extol it. Ibn Ashur says faith, virtues, courage and learning require it, citing 103:1–3, 32:24, 7:137, 2:153, a saying attributed to Ali and Zufar's verse. Ghazali counts over seventy Qur'anic mentions and describes human patience as unique between instinct-driven animals and perfected angels. Hafiz's ruby couplet stresses its cost."}, {"id": "2:45/q06/p2", "position": "Patience is a means of receiving God's gift of patience and great good.", "reasons": "The Durr reports God grants patience to one seeking it, with no better gift, while Umar calls it the best life and Maymun says great good requires it."}]}
{"id": "2:45/q07", "question": "What does الصلاة mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether الصلاة names the ritual, the Arabic sense of supplication, or inward communion.", "positions": [{"id": "2:45/q07/p1", "position": "Ritual prayer, including prescribed and, on one account, voluntary forms.", "reasons": "Qurtubi and Ibn Ashur make it the ritual act; Mujahid in Abu Hayyan includes obligatory, sunnah and optional prayers. Baydawi catalogs purification, covering, spending, qibla, bodily worship, intention, recitation, testimony, and abstention. Muqatil and Durr stress guarding times and postures. Alusi considers the alternative supplication reading strained."}, {"id": "2:45/q07/p2", "position": "Supplication or earnest asking God for relief.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi and Nasafi align it with steadfastness and remembrance in 8:45; Abu Hayyan says the construction may imply an omitted term. {"id": "2:45/q08", "question": "How do patience and prayer provide help?", "turns_on": "What causal or spiritual work the two practices perform.", "positions": [{"id": "2:45/q08/p1", "position": "Prayer's recitation, remembrance, and discipline turn one toward God and the Hereafter and restrain wrong, while patience curbs desire.", "reasons": "Tabari, Zajjaj, Wahidi, Jishumi, Razi, Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and others cite 29:45 and describe recitation of promise and warning, reflection, admonition, humility, and resistance to leadership and greed. Wahidi says fasting curbs greed while prayer curbs arrogance. Baydawi, Alusi, Elmalili and Kur'an Yolu add purification, lifelong relation to God, trust, repair of hardship and moral resolve. Study Quran contrasts deferred gratification with prayer's retreat from worldly occupation."}, {"id": "2:45/q08/p2", "position": "Their combination joins the strongest inward act with the strongest bodily act.", "reasons": "Jishumi and Tabarsi present patience as the great act of the heart and prayer as the great act of the limbs; Ibn Ashur makes them patience and gratitude. Sulami and Qushayri describe patience's inward withdrawal paired with prayer's presence."}, {"id": "2:45/q08/p3", "position": "True help is from God; the practices dispose the person to receive it.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says tasks exceed individual strength, patience shrinks calamity, and prayer awakens faith in God's support. Qashani denies independent human power; Sulami reports that believers achieve both only with God's help."}]}
